docs.title: Large Hadron Collider
docs.text:
The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN is a circular particle accelerator with a circumference of approximately 27 km.

It accelerates two counter-rotating beams of particles before bringing them into collision at designated interaction points.

docs.title: Accelerator complex
docs.text:
Particles are accelerated through several stages before being injected into the LHC.

For protons, the main acceleration chain consists of Linac4, the Proton Synchrotron Booster (PSB), the Proton Synchrotron (PS), and the Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS).

Figure 1: The CERN accelerator complex, layout in 2022. Source: CERN.

docs.title: Experiments at the LHC
docs.text:
The counter-rotating particle beams are brought into collision at designated interaction points along the accelerator ring.

The particles produced in these collisions are measured by different detector systems, allowing the underlying physical processes to be reconstructed.

docs.title: Major experiments
docs.text:
Experiment Primary research objectives ALICE Heavy-ion physics, QCD and quark-gluon plasma ATLAS Higgs physics, Standard Model measurements and searches for new physics CMS Higgs physics, precision measurements and searches beyond the Standard Model LHCb Heavy-flavour physics, CP violation and rare decays

ATLAS and CMS are general-purpose experiments, whereas ALICE and LHCb focus on more specialised research programmes.

Figure 2: Collision events recorded by ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb in 2026. Source: CERN.

docs.title: Collision systems
docs.text:
The LHC enables the investigation of different physical processes through various collision systems.

Proton–protonLead–leadProton–lead

Proton–proton (pp) collisions are used to study fundamental particle interactions, perform precision measurements and search for new particles.

Lead–lead (Pb–Pb) collisions allow the investigation of strongly interacting matter under extreme conditions, including the formation and properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

Proton–lead (p–Pb) collisions provide an important reference system for investigating nuclear effects and understanding the properties of small collision systems.

docs.title: Regular Expressions
docs.text: Regular expressions (regex) provide a compact way to search, filter and validate textual data. In scientific computing, they are particularly useful for processing log files, extracting numerical values and selecting relevant data.

docs.title: Basic metacharacters
docs.text: Metacharacter Meaning . Any single character * Zero or more occurrences + One or more occurrences ? Zero or one occurrence ^ Beginning of a line $ End of a line [abc] Character inclusion [^abc] Character exclusion {n} Exactly n repetitions \| Alternation

docs.title: Combining conditions
docs.text:
Multiple regular expressions can be combined using logical operations.

Let \(A\) and \(B\) denote the sets of strings matching two regular expressions.

A logical AND corresponds to the intersection

\[ A \land B \quad \longleftrightarrow \quad A \cap B. \]

In the shell, this can be implemented using pipes:

grep -E 'regex1' file.txt | grep -E 'regex2'

A logical OR corresponds to the union

\[ A \lor B \quad \longleftrightarrow \quad A \cup B. \]

This can be implemented using alternation:

grep -E 'regex1|regex2' file.txt

docs.title: Numerical input validation
docs.text:
Scientific data often contain floating-point numbers written in scientific notation. The following regular expression validates decimal numbers with an optional exponent:

grep -E '^[+-]?[0-9]*\.[0-9]+(e[+-]?[0-9]+)?$' floats.txt

Examples of accepted input:

  • 8.54585
  • -0.54585
  • .54585
  • 8.54585e-2
  • 008.54585e+002

This allows numerical input to be checked before further processing or analysis.

docs.title: Basic vs. Extended Regular Expressions
docs.text:
The grep command supports two regular expression syntaxes: Basic Regular Expressions (BRE) and Extended Regular Expressions (ERE).

By default, grep uses BRE, whereas grep -E uses ERE. They differ mainly in the interpretation of certain metacharacters.

docs.title: Repetition
docs.text:
Match strings consisting of exactly three digits.

BREERE

Basic Regular Expressions (BRE)

grep '^[0-9]\{3\}$' file.txt

In BRE, the curly brackets must be escaped using backslashes to indicate repetition.

Extended Regular Expressions (ERE)

grep -E '^[0-9]{3}$' file.txt

In ERE, curly brackets are interpreted directly as repetition operators.

Syntax breakdown:

Expression Meaning ^ Beginning of the line [0-9] Any digit between 0 and 9 {3} Exactly three occurrences $ End of the line

Syntax breakdown:

Expression Meaning ^ Beginning of the line [0-9] Any digit between 0 and 9 {3} Exactly three occurrences $ End of the line

docs.title: Grouping and alternation
docs.text:
Match strings consisting of either abc or def.

BREERE

Basic Regular Expressions (BRE)

grep '^\(abc\|def\)$' file.txt

Grouping and alternation are expressed using escaped parentheses and an escaped vertical bar.

Extended Regular Expressions (ERE)

grep -E '^(abc|def)$' file.txt

Parentheses and the vertical bar are interpreted directly as grouping and alternation operators.

Syntax breakdown:

Expression Meaning ^ Beginning of the line ( ... ) Groups multiple expressions abc First possible match \| Logical OR (alternation) def Second possible match $ End of the line

Compatibility

Alternation in BRE using \| is an extension to the POSIX standard. Its availability depends on the grep implementation.

docs.title: Interactive regex playground
docs.text:
Construct your own regular expressions and test them against the examples below.

Challenge Wordle challenge Integer validation Floating-point numbers Custom expression Regular expression Ignore case Test strings

The interactive regex playground is available in the online documentation.

Regular expression engine

This playground uses JavaScript regular expressions. Its syntax and behaviour may differ from POSIX BRE and ERE as implemented by grep.

docs.title: Git & Version Control
docs.text:
Git is a distributed version control system that records changes in project files and enables reproducible software development.

In scientific computing, it allows analysis code to be tracked, compared and restored throughout a project.

docs.title: Repository structure
docs.text:
Git distinguishes between four principal components:

Component Purpose Working directory Files currently being edited Staging area Changes selected for the next commit Local repository Recorded commits and project history Remote repository Shared repository hosted on a server

docs.title: Git workflow
docs.text:
Changes are prepared locally, committed and subsequently synchronized with a remote repository.

Fetch versus pull

git fetch retrieves remote commits without integrating them into the current branch.

git pull fetches remote changes and integrates them into the current branch.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text: Command Function git clone Create a local copy of a repository git status Inspect the repository state git add Stage changes git commit Record staged changes git push Publish local commits git fetch Retrieve remote commits git pull Retrieve and integrate remote changes git diff Inspect changes git log Display commit history

docs.text:

docs.text:
git add .
git commit -m "Update documentation"
git push
ENABLE_PDF_EXPORT=1 mkdocs gh-deploy

Development workflow

PDF generation is disabled during normal development to reduce build times. It is enabled explicitly when generating or deploying the complete documentation.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Programming tools play an important role in experimental high-energy physics, from processing large datasets to maintaining reproducible analysis workflows.

This documentation introduces selected tools and demonstrates their application through short practical examples.
